2003–2008: Athens.
Five unforgettable years in a city that shaped me.
Athens taught me how to live on my own, to discover who I am, and to grow into the woman I am today. I carry so many precious moments from that time—memories that still warm my heart.

When I left, I chose not to return too soon. Whenever I traveled, I always chased new destinations… and so, somehow, seventeen years passed before I came back.

But this time, I returned!
A different chapter, a different version of myself.
And suddenly I remembered exactly why I fell in love with this city,
and why it has remained one of my favorites all these years.

 We entered the open building that was lined by antiques,  real pretty beautiful antiques, if I lived closer I would have beeen tempted to buy a few things.

Anyway we found the lift and up we went….. 6th floor.
 OMG- I wish we had found it sooner on our trip and I would have been up there every day for either lunch or dinner- a beautiful bar/ restaurant/ rooftop!!! Loved the style and decor and sooo chillaxing. There was even a double swing BUT I didn’t trust myself on it so stayed out on a chair.

We both ordered our coffees, I removed my ‘Suresmile’ retainers and chilled in the sunshine and gentle breeze.

More than two decades later, when longtime owner Frank Case passed away and The Algonquin was put up for sale, Ben made good on his promise, purchasing the hotel in 1946 as a lasting tribute to their love. Today, their story lives on as part of The Algonquin’s enduring legacy of romance and history in the heart of New York City.

caption:
As a walking tour guide in Manhattan I see a good portion of the island on a regular basis, but it's always fun to stumble upon a temporary art exhibit of a well-known artist.

The Algonquin Hotel recently hosted the exhibit "Strokes of Genius: The Works of Al Hirschfeld" in their Oak Room.

Al Hirschfeld (1903 - 2003) was a renowned American caricaturist and graphic artist known for his dynamic pen-and-ink drawings of theater and public figures that captured the essence of his subjects with a signature fluid line. 

His iconic artwork, which he produced for over 75 years, most notably for The New York Times, was characterized by its elegant simplicity and ability to convey emotion through a single line. 

After the birth of his daughter Nina, he famously hid her name within the lines of his drawings.

caption: Spent the better part of the day wandering around Brooklyn’s waterfront. Ate dinner at Cecconi’s and talked travel with the bartender Patrick who is originally from San Francisco. Watched the sunset from a spot he recommended. Was going to take the subway back to midtown but impulsively got off in the West Village. Walked a lot. Nightlife was booming and a little intimidating because of the sheer quantity of people. Stopped in One if By Land, Two if By Sea which has been on my radar a long time. Got the chocolate soufflé. Worth the $25. The piano player set the mood. Walked around Bryant Park for a while before heading back to The Algonquin. Changed into comfy clothes and am now sitting in the lobby reading, while all the drinkers pile back in from their nights out to continue the party at the hotel bar. There’s always a twinge of sadness in my NY trips because it makes me so incredibly happy that it also makes me hyper aware that I have to leave eventually. But for now, my heart is full from a great day. 🩷

We saw 2025 year end list fav @yhwhnailgun onstage last week @babysallright for @marshall. Just like last time we caught them, singer Zack Borzoi doesn’t perform so much as enter a state. 

He’s described that state as “feeling in raw form, an emotion that can then go in six different ways.” Watching it live, you believe him. 

Per @pitch “In Borzone’s lyrics are the dark strains of industrial rock, explorations of self-lacerating pain, and recurring motifs of skin, wings, and nothingness. His subcutaneous writing fits the band’s subterranean sound: Everything raw worth expressing is within, deeper and deeper still.”

Live, his body slackens, then sharpens. Eyes unfocused. Movements slow, then sudden. Everything feels intentional, but not rehearsed. Like he’s letting something move through him rather than trying to control it.

The music carries weight without explanation. Dark textures. Physical lyrics. Repeated symbols that feel more felt than understood. It’s less about meaning and more about release.

Sometimes the body says what language can’t.

Earlier this year I saw Cursive open up for Bright Eyes at the Brooklyn Paramount. I dubbed this the year of Saddle Creek, swooning to the bands that soundtracked my high school years and continue to be on rotation in my music library over the course of the last 20 years. I smiled as I came across their music in my old CD collection, which I retrieved this summer from the house I grew up in. I laughed to myself when I wore my Cursive shirt to Rilo Kiley’s reunion tour. I was content. 🎵 THIS is the latest from Saddle Creek…

And then, Cursive announced a headlining club tour to close out the year. I had to get tickets as soon as they went on sale, I wanted to be up front and I wanted to photograph them again. I wanted to time travel through the music to the way it made me feel when I was listening to them for the first time. 

I first photographed Cursive in 2015 when they played Saint Vitus during their Ugly Organ anniversary shows. I was fairly new to concert photography at the time and I remember being so happy with my captures but it literally took me a decade to share them. (Check my grid to see). So, it was important to me that this time around, I get them up quickly.

Copiava referências, me vestia igual todo mundo.

Na prática… era como se eu tivesse desaparecido.

O problema nunca foi a roupa.
Foi usar o que não dizia nada sobre mim.

Você pode estar se apagando e culpando seu corpo…
quando, na real, o problema é que suas roupas não contam sua história.

	4.	Você precisa de aprovação o tempo todo.
Se pergunta: “Será que tá bom?” em vez de “Isso é minha cara!”
	5.	Você se sente neutra demais.

The celebration then naturally unfolded at the reception venue in the heart of a famous Capital — a historic landmark, one of the oldest banks in New York, offering breathtaking views and a truly iconic atmosphere.
It was a genuine winter wedding: cold, windy, and cinematic. We captured striking, dramatic frames in front of the capital, embracing the season and the city’s timeless grandeur.

The wedding itself was magnificent and grand in every sense — filled with incredible energy, top-tier entertainment, exceptional cuisine, and nonstop joy.
Overall, it was a top-of-the-line luxury wedding day.

Diana and Alex were an absolute dream to work with — fun, easy-going, full of warmth, and completely present in every moment. Their effortless chemistry and joyful energy set the tone for the entire day.

A truly beautiful way to close the 2025 wedding season.
